fixes.explanation: Verse 30 says there was loud wailing in Egypt, "for there was no house without someone dead." I think this is one of the heavy parts of the story, and it's okay to let it be heavy for a moment. The sound that night was grief, spreading through the whole land.

Pharaoh, Egypt's king, tells Moses, Israel's leader, and Aaron, his brother (Exodus 4:14), "Get up, leave my people, both you and the Israelites! Go, worship the LORD as you have requested." Back in Exodus 5:2 he said he would not let Israel go. I think he was done bargaining, friend. Now he's the one doing the pushing.

Pharaoh, Egypt's king, doesn't ask Moses, Israel's leader, and Aaron, his brother (Exodus 4:14), to wait for anything. He says, "Get up, leave my people, both you and the Israelites!" Nobody says "Get up!" and then "Take your time." It's still night, and he wants them gone.

Pharaoh, Egypt's king, did once say something like that, back when he told them to sacrifice to their God in the land (Exodus 8:25). Not this time. Now he tells Moses, Israel's leader, and Aaron, his brother (Exodus 4:14), "Go, worship the LORD as you have requested." The offer to stay is gone.

It's actually True, friend. Pharaoh says, "Take your flocks and herds as well, just as you have said, and depart!" (Exodus 12:32) Earlier he wanted the flocks and herds left behind (Exodus 10:24). Same Pharaoh, new answer.
He ends with, "And bless me also." (Exodus 12:32) Think about that. Back in Exodus 5:2 he said, "I do not know the LORD," and now he wants a blessing on his way out the door. That's quite a turn.

The three-day journey shows up earlier, when Moses and Aaron asked Pharaoh to let them take one into the wilderness (Exodus 5:3). Pharaoh doesn't ask them to come back at all. His last words to them are, "And bless me also." (Exodus 12:32)

Verse 34 says the people took their dough before it was leavened, carrying it on their shoulders in kneading bowls wrapped in clothing. My mustache handles cookie boxes all day, but a whole bowl of dough? I'd have dough all over my chef's hat. These folks were on the move.

It's actually False. The Israelites asked the Egyptians for articles of silver and gold, and for clothing. Then "the LORD gave the people such favor in the sight of the Egyptians that they granted their request." (Exodus 12:35-36) The Egyptians said yes, not no.

The Israelites asked for articles of silver and gold, and for clothing, and the Egyptians said yes (Exodus 12:35-36). The text says, "In this way they plundered the Egyptians." That's the opposite of being turned down, baker.
Verse 37 says the Israelites journeyed from Rameses to Succoth. The text adds about 600,000 men on foot, besides women and children. That's a whole lot of people on one road.

Bethel is where Jacob, Isaac's son (Genesis 25:26), had a dream and named the place (Genesis 28:12, 19). It isn't where they're going here. The text says the Israelites journeyed from Rameses to Succoth.

Hebron is where Abram, whom God later renamed Abraham (Genesis 17:5), lived by the oaks of Mamre (Genesis 13:18). But that isn't the place named here. Verse 37 says the Israelites journeyed from Rameses to Succoth.
It's actually False. Verse 39 says the people "…had not prepared any provisions for themselves." Nobody got a head start on packing. That's a timer nobody got to set.

The text says the people "…had not prepared any provisions for themselves." (Exodus 12:39) Their dough had no leaven, so they baked what they had brought out of Egypt into unleavened loaves. I've scrambled to finish a batch before the timer, but never with a deadline like this.

Verse 39 says, "For when they had been driven out of Egypt, they could not delay and had not prepared any provisions for themselves." They were driven out, and they couldn't delay. Preparing provisions was the part that didn't happen.
Verse 41 says, "At the end of the 430 years, to the very day, all the LORD’s divisions went out of the land of Egypt." To the very day, friend. After 430 years, the text still counts the day.

Verse 50 says, "Then all the Israelites did this—they did just as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron." Moses, Israel's leader, and Aaron, his brother (Exodus 4:14), were the ones who received the command. The people did just what He said.
